title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance (Canonical Extended)
author: Maya Chen
body:
Purpose
-------
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance, and the ADR (architecture decision record) process. It is intended for engineering teams, tech leads, and platform owners to provide a single source of truth for decisions, mandatory controls, and recommended best practices.

Scope
-----
Applies to: all services and components that participate in customer-facing inference (hosted API, Dedicated, Private), supporting infra (CI/CD, networking, secrets), and developer-facing libraries (SDKs, internal CLIs).

Principles
----------
- Predictability: prioritize stable contracts and measurable SLOs.
- Developer ergonomics: conventions that minimize cognitive overhead (consistent patterns, linters, templates).
- Production-first: defaults favor reliability, observability, and security.
- Incremental evolution: use ADRs for irreversible or wide-impact changes.

1) API Standards
----------------
Intro: APIs are the contract between Redwood and customers and between services. Maintain backward compatibility and clear versioning.

Key rules:
- Use OpenAPI v3 for all public REST surfaces. Store spec in the same repo as the service under /api/openapi.yaml.
- Versioning: Major versions only for breaking changes (x.Y.Z). Minor/patch for additive changes and fixes.
- Resource naming: kebab-case for path segments, nouns for resources, avoid verbs. Example: /v1/models/{model_id}/deployments.
- HTTP semantics: use 2xx for success, 4xx for client errors, 5xx for server errors; prefer 409 for conflict, 429 for rate-limited, 503 for transient upstream failures.
- Error schema: standardize on: { code, message, details? }. Provide machine-readable error codes (lower_snake_case). Example: {
  "code": "model_not_found",
  "message": "Model not found: my-model"
}
- Pagination: cursor-based pagination for large result sets.
- Rate limiting: clients receive X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, Retry-After headers.
- Authentication: service-to-service use mTLS or short-lived JWT. Public API use RBAC-backed API keys with scoped claims.
- API review: any public or cross-team API change must go through the API review checklist (PR template + OpenAPI diff + compatibility test).

Example OpenAPI snippet:
```yaml
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Redwood Models API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /v1/models/{model_id}:
    get:
      summary: Get model metadata
      parameters:
        - name: model_id
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
      responses:
        '200':
          description: OK
```

2) Coding Standards
-------------------
Purpose: maintainable, reviewable, and testable code across services and SDKs.

Rules:
- Languages & frameworks: prefer Go for core runtime services, Python for infra and ML ops tooling, TypeScript for console and web SDKs. Exceptions require ADR.
- Formatting & linting: enforce gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, Black/ruff for Python, Prettier/ESLint for TS. CI must fail on linter errors.
- Testing: aim for >70% coverage for service-critical packages; require unit tests for all new logic and integration tests for public APIs.
- PR process: small PRs (<400 lines), include rationale, link ADRs/design docs, include changelog entry when public behavior changes.
- Dependency management: pin exact versions (go.mod, poetry.lock, package-lock.json). Security patches apply within 72 hours for high severity.

3) Infrastructure Standards
-------------------------
Goals: reproducible, auditable, and secure infrastructure.

Rules:
- IaC: Terraform for cloud resources. Store state in a centrally managed backend (S3 + DynamoDB for locking). Modules must be reviewed and published in the internal registry.
- Environments: enforce separation of dev, staging, prod accounts/projects. Networking isolation between prod and non-prod by default.
- Secrets: use KMS + secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault for Private). No plaintext secrets in repos.
- CI/CD: pipelines must run unit tests, linters, static analysis, and integration tests for canary environments before production rollout.
- Capacity & autoscaling: define horizontal and vertical scaling rules per service; include safety caps to avoid uncontrolled growth.

Config table (example):
| Component | Min capacity (prod) | Scale metric | Owner |
|----------|---------------------:|--------------|-------|
| inference-runtime | 4 nodes | queue_latency_p99 > 200ms | infra-team |
| api-gateway | 2 instances | CPU > 60% | platform |

4) Model-Serving Standards
-------------------------
Scope: how models are packaged, deployed, and served across Redwood hosted, Dedicated, and Private modes.

Standards:
- Model packaging: prefer standard tarball containing model weights, config.json, and a manifest.json with schema: { name, version, created_at, checksum, required_runtime }.
- Quantization: document quantization profile in manifest (e.g., int8, fp16) and run evaluation on representative prompt sets before promotion.
- Inference runtime contract: every model must expose a health endpoint (/health) and a metadata endpoint (/v1/metadata).
- KV cache and warmup: large models must support KV-prefill hooks in the runtime; cold-start mitigation via async prefill jobs.
- Rollouts: use canary by traffic-weight (default 5% for 24h) + automatic rollback on error-rate or quality-regression. Quality checks must run using the model's canonical prompt-set.
- Telemetry: model-level metrics emitted: tokens_generated, tok_latency_p50/p95/p99, model_errors, cache_hit_rate.

5) Observability Standards
-------------------------
Goals: fast detection and diagnosis of incidents with minimal cognitive load.

Metrics:
- Emit prometheus-style metrics with stable metric names and labels: service, route, model, region, environment.
- Required SLOs (example): request_latency_p95 < 250ms, error_rate_p99 < 0.1% for control plane operations.

Logging & Tracing:
- Structured JSON logs with fields: timestamp, service, trace_id, span_id, level, msg, route, user_id (if present).
- Traces: instrument critical paths (request ingress -> router -> runtime -> model), sample at 1% by default and 100% for traces flagged by errors.

Dashboards & Alerts:
- Per-route dashboards with latency percentiles, error rates, and token throughput.
- Alert rules: page SRE for P1 (SLO burn > 50% in 1h or production 5xx > 1% for 5m). Pager rotation and runbooks must be linked from alerts.

6) Performance Standards
-----------------------
Targets & Testing:
- SLO definitions: teams must publish SLOs per public-facing route and per-model inference SLA. Example SLO table: 
| Route | SLO | Objective | Error budget | Owner |
| /v1/generate | Availability 99.9% | p95 latency < 300ms | 43.2 minutes/month | model-ops |

- Load testing: scheduling cadence quarterly for major services and per-release for changes that alter resource usage. Use synthetic traffic that mirrors customer distribution including sequence length and batching patterns.
- Benchmarking: runtime teams maintain reproducible benchmark harnesses and baseline perf profiles for each supported model/quantization combo. Benchmarks must include tokens/sec, memory, and p99 latency versus sequence length.

7) ADRs and Decision Process
---------------------------
When to write an ADR:
- Anytime a choice has long-term cost/ops implications (e.g., new storage system, major API contract change, language/platform shift).

ADRs must include:
- Title and short summary.
- Context and alternatives considered.
- Decision and rationale.
- Consequences and migration plan.
- Owners and reviewers.

Workflow:
1. Draft ADR in repo under /docs/adrs with a template.
2. Tag reviewers and link to relevant design docs.
3. After approval, publish to Confluence and update related code/infra (e.g., lint rules, templates).

8) Ownership, Reviews, and Enforcement
-----------------------------------
- Each standard area has an owning working group (API Guild, Runtime WG, Infra Ops, Observability Guild). Owners are responsible for keeping standards up-to-date and running biweekly office hours for consults.
- Enforcement: CI gates + periodic audits. Non-compliant services receive 30-day remediation plans.

Appendices
---------
- Templates: ADR template, API review checklist, OpenAPI linting rules (links).
- Example SLO definition sample (YAML):
```yaml
slo_name: v1-generate-latency
objective: p95 < 300ms
window: 30d
owner: model-ops
```
